meta.howToRead: Each domain/audience object has the requested fields plus 'evidence' (strength + what is sourced vs inferred) and 'sourceIds' pointing into the 'sources' array. 'Strong' means directly supported by named research or a named benchmark. 'Moderate' means partly sourced and partly synthesized. 'Thin' means mostly synthesized from adjacent sources.
cautions: Conversion benchmarks (Unbounce, First Page Sage, RevenueCat) are vendor datasets from their own customers' pages or apps, not random samples. Use them for relative comparison, not as targets.
Several figures were reachable only through secondary summaries of the original report. Those are labeled 'via' in the source list.
typicalSections, toneRange and proofTypes are synthesized patterns. The sources support the direction of each pattern, not every item on the list.

domains.conversionPattern: free_trial or free_workout_sample > paid_plan; the first session must deliver a workout, because trial cancellations concentrate on Day 0
commonObjections: Too expensive: 41% of former US gym members who cancelled cited cost, the top reason
No time (23%) or life change (25%)
I can get results on my own (19%)
Fear of paying for something I will not use: in a study of 7,752 members, people on flat monthly fees over $70 attended about 4.3 times a month
Will this work for someone like me? (inferred; results credibility)

evidence.note: Objections are sourced (YouGov, DellaVigna & Malmendier). The trial pattern is sourced to app-store data (RevenueCat), which may differ from web-only funnels. Unbounce (2020) found fitness and nutrition pages were the wordiest of 16 industries, which describes what marketers do, not what converts. Section list and proof types are inferred.

domains.conversionPattern: learn_more > assessment_or_consultation_or_free_trial > subscription_or_purchase; the 2024 Unbounce median for health and wellness pages is 5.1%
commonObjections: Can I trust this source? In a longitudinal study, users quickly rejected sales sites and sometimes rejected good content because of poor design
Is it safe, and will my doctor agree? Participants still treated the physician as the primary authority
Is this for someone like me? Personalized stories from like-minded others raised trust
What happens to my data (inferred; no source retrieved)
Cost and commitment

evidence.note: Trust mechanics come from Sillence et al. (n=15 women, one health topic) and Fogg et al. (n=2,684; design look cited in 46.1% of credibility comments; a companion expert study covered health and finance sites). The conversion pattern is inferred.

domains.conversionPattern: sign_up (short form, progressive data requests) > funded_account_or_first_transaction; for B2B fintech: demo > pilot > contract. The 2024 Unbounce median for financial services pages is 8.3%
commonObjections: Do I trust this site with payment or personal data? 17–25% of US checkout abandoners cited this in Baymard's surveys
Hidden fees and unclear total cost (extra costs is the top checkout abandonment reason at 39–48%)
How long will this take and what documents do I need? (inferred)
Can I reach a human if something goes wrong? A Ferpection benchmark of 10 French banking sites found human contact a core trust factor
Is this company legitimate and regulated? (inferred)

evidence.note: I found no fintech-specific pattern library or peer-reviewed conversion study. The domain is triangulated from Fogg et al. (finance was one of 10 tested categories), Baymard (payment trust), Unbounce (median rate) and a vendor benchmark. Regulatory-badge conventions are practice, not researched here.

domains.conversionPattern: opt_in_free_trial or freemium > demo_request > contact_sales; in First Page Sage's data, visitor-to-trial is 8.5% with 18.2% trial-to-paid (opt-in), versus 2.5% and 48.8% for opt-out (card required), and 13.3% and 2.6% for freemium
commonObjections: Where is the pricing? NN/g found pricing was the most-wanted B2B information and users left sites that hid it
Will it integrate, and is it secure and compliant?
Internal buy-in: buying groups typically involve 6–10 stakeholders and need a business justification
Is the website consistent with what sales says? 69% of surveyed B2B buyers reported discrepancies (Gartner)
Switching cost and time to value (inferred)

evidence.note: Best-evidenced domain: NN/g B2B research (293 sites tested), Gartner buyer surveys, and multiple benchmarks. Trial-model numbers come from one vendor's dataset via a secondary summary; other summaries with different figures exist, so treat them as directional. SaaS was the hardest-to-read industry in Unbounce's 2020 analysis.

domains.conversionPattern: product_view > add_to_cart > guest_checkout > optional account after purchase; Baymard puts average cart abandonment near 70% and estimates about 35% conversion upside from checkout redesign at an average large site
commonObjections: Extra costs at checkout (39–48% of abandoners, depending on survey year)
Forced account creation (19–26%)
Do not trust the site with my card (17–25%)
Delivery too slow (21–24%)
Checkout too long or complicated (17–22%)
Cannot see total cost up front (14–21%)
Returns policy unsatisfactory (12–18%)

evidence.note: Baymard percentages vary by survey year and by which secondary source reports them, hence the ranges. Spiegel Research Center (Northwestern): a product with five reviews had 270% higher purchase likelihood than one with none (380% for higher-priced products, 190% for lower-priced), and purchase likelihood peaked at ratings of 4.0–4.7, not 5.0. Unbounce's 2024 ecommerce median is 4.2%, and its per-industry medians are known here only through Backlinko's summary.

domains.conversionPattern: order_or_reserve (one tap) > repeat_order_or_subscription > loyalty; reduce friction at the first three points users struggle with
commonObjections: Where is it, and is it open? Finding a location was one of the top three problems in ordering usability tests
Starting an order and selecting menu items were the other two top problems (MeasuringU, 180 participants across major chains)
Delivery fees and price (inferred)
Dietary and allergen information (inferred)
Can I skip or cancel a subscription easily? (inferred)

evidence.note: Only the ordering-friction findings (MeasuringU) and the copy-simplicity observation (Unbounce 2020: catering and restaurant pages had the simplest copy of 16 industries) are directly sourced. Section list, tone and proof types are largely inferred. A DoorDash merchant blog claims 87% of consumers chose a dish based on an appealing photo. That is a vendor claim I could not trace to a study, so I have not relied on it.

domains.conversionPattern: request_info_form or scholarship_calculator > visit_or_tour_or_free_preview > apply_or_enroll; the 2024 Unbounce median for education pages is 8.4%
commonObjections: Cost and financial aid (top content sought after academics in RNL's surveys)
Cannot find information about the program I want: about 1 in 4 prospective students reported this (RNL 2025; 22% in 2023)
Will it lead to an outcome such as a job or degree? (inferred)
Is it credible and accredited? (inferred)
Does it fit my life and schedule? (inferred)

evidence.note: Strong for higher-ed recruitment (RNL E-Expectations surveys: 1,500+ US high-school students in 2025, 2,000+ in 2023; 91–93% use college websites; top contact route is a website form; students are willing to share email, name, cell, and parent contact details; 82% watch videos; 73% use virtual tours). Evidence for online-course marketplaces and edtech is not covered by these sources.

domains.conversionPattern: wishlist_or_follow > demo_or_playtest > purchase_or_download; a Steam-style page is judged in seconds from the capsule image, a short trailer or gif, the short description and the first few screenshots
commonObjections: What kind of game is this, and what do I do in it? The capsule and short description must answer immediately
Does the gameplay look and feel good? (screenshots and trailer carry this)
Will it run on my machine? (system requirements; inferred)
Is it worth the price? Reviews and negative reviews get skimmed (Zukowski)
Monetization or bug concerns such as pay-to-win or early access (inferred)

evidence.note: Directional only. Valve's Steamworks documentation defines page structure (capsules, short description, longer 'About This Game' lower on the page, keep image text minimal because it must be localized). Zukowski's Game Developer article (2019) describes one observed Steam session in which a user wishlisted after the capsule, watched about 13 seconds of an animated preview, read 12 words of the short description, skipped the trailer, and looked at 4 screenshots in about 5.5 seconds. That is an illustrative case, not a population average. I found no rigorous conversion benchmark for game pages, and Unbounce's 'events and entertainment' median (12.3%) is not a games benchmark.

domains.conversionPattern: brand_immersion > book_appointment_or_contact_client_advisor > purchase (online or in boutique); three in four luxury purchases are influenced by online activity even when completed in store
commonObjections: Authenticity and counterfeit risk (inferred)
Does buying online cheapen the experience? (inferred from the tension between exclusivity and online availability discussed in the luxury digital literature)
Price justification: one lab study found displaying prices can raise perceived luxury in the premium segment, contrary to folk wisdom
Service, delivery and after-care: product information, convenience and responsive customer service influenced revisit intent on luxury fashion sites (Korean sample, n=292)

evidence.note: Sourced: McKinsey/Altagamma digital influence figures; an IJRDM 2013 study of 81 luxury homepages (darker backgrounds, large or full-screen stage content, horizontal navigation, substantially fewer elements; lab experiment showed perceived luxury effects, but no conversion measured; I could not confirm the author list); Choi, Kim & Lee (2015). The price-display study is a single experiment. Everything else is synthesis. Spiegel's review data suggests reviews matter more at higher prices, but luxury brands often omit reviews, so I do not list them as a standard luxury proof type.

domains.conversionPattern: single_primary_cta > low_friction_form_or_click_through; keep the promise and the first screen aligned, since 57% of viewing time is above the fold and 74% falls within the first two screenfuls
commonObjections: What is this, and why should I care? (inferred)
Can I trust it? Design look was cited in 46.1% of credibility judgments in Fogg et al.
What does it cost, and how much effort is it? (inferred)

evidence.note: NN/g eyetracking (about 130,000 fixations, 120 participants) supports the above-the-fold pattern. Unbounce data (as summarized by Apexure) reports pages written at a 5th–7th grade reading level converting at about 11% versus 5% for 'professional' copy. That is a vendor finding via a secondary source. Overall Unbounce 2024 median is 6.6% across industries.

modifies.buyer: Parent or guardian. NN/g likens this to B2B, where purchasers and decision makers are not the users
trustSignals: Clear statement of no ads and no in-app purchases in the child's flow
Age-appropriate design and privacy defaults (UK ICO Children's Code: high-privacy defaults, no nudging children to give data)
Evidence-based learning claims (active, engaging, meaningful, socially interactive)
avoid: Manipulative design: about 80% of apps used by 3–5-year-olds in one study had at least one such feature
Ads or promos indistinguishable from content
Touch targets under about 2 cm x 2 cm and precision dragging
Long instructional text, redundant navigation, and required scrolling for the youngest
Content pitched even one school grade off the child's level
Decorated symbols such as progress bars for under-4s
Motion that is decorative rather than tied to the story or task

evidence.note: Detailed in the earlier children's findings: NN/g (125 children tested across 2001, 2010, 2018), Takacs et al. meta-analysis, Radesky et al., Hiniker et al., ICO Code. Motion is 'medium' because children like animation and sound but distracting extras hurt comprehension. 'High' contrast is a design judgment (bright, saturated colors plus at least AA text contrast), not a directly tested value.

modifies.buyer: Teens research and influence, but a parent or other adult typically holds the payment method (NN/g: teens visit ecommerce sites to research products and build wish lists for credit-card-carrying adults)
trustSignals: Real content and stories from other teens
Visible privacy control with no forced public profiles
avoid: The word 'kid' or condescending, babyish tone
Pop-ups and long waits
Dense text; NN/g found teens read poorly and prefer scannable, visual content
Precision interactions on touch devices such as dropdowns, drag-and-drop, rollovers and small click zones
Glitzy blinking graphics and pointless multimedia
Forced registration that makes a profile public
Tiny fonts, which bothered teens as much as adults

evidence.note: NN/g research with 100 teens over three rounds, 210 websites and 30 apps. Teen task success was below adults' in the older 2005 study, partly due to reading skill, research strategy and patience. The 16px minimum is inferred from NN/g's finding that teens dislike small type like adults do.

modifies.buyer: The visitor themselves (or a household decision); assumed default when no other decision maker is indicated
avoid: Forced account creation before purchase
Autoplay sound and animation
Pop-ups and heavy promotions (NN/g: adults avoid ads and view promos skeptically)
Long text without scan support (adults scan)
Hidden costs

evidence.note: NN/g's age comparison tables give 12 pt (16 px) type, scanning behavior, dislike of animation and sound, and ad avoidance. Trust signals are drawn from Baymard and Spiegel and apply mainly to shopping contexts.

modifies.buyer: The older adult, who is typically self-directed in the NN/g tasks (banking, shopping, health, travel). Influence from adult children or caregivers is plausible but was not evidenced in the sources reviewed
trustSignals: Phone number and human help clearly visible
Plain language with technical terms defined
Minimal data requests, since today's older users delete accounts that collect too much
avoid: Tiny text and low-contrast text (aim for at least 4.5:1, ideally 7:1)
Pull-down and hierarchical hover menus
Unlabeled icons
Unforgiving forms and vague error messages
Pop-ups and autoplay sound
Drastic navigation changes
Auto-advancing carousels and heavy page clutter
Framing older people as a niche

evidence.note: Detailed in the earlier seniors findings: Bernard et al. (14 pt), Jin et al. (touch targets), WCAG contrast rationale (20/40 acuity near age 80), NN/g (Nielsen 2013; Kane 2019), W3C WAI-AGE. NN/g's own floor for senior sites is 12 pt; 19 px reflects the 14 pt result in Bernard et al.

modifies.buyer: The parent, who acts as purchaser and gatekeeper for products used by children; they often consult a doctor (61% in Pew's survey of parents of children 11 or younger) and other parents (55%) before deciding
trustSignals: Evidence-based claims rather than generic 'educational' labels
avoid: Unsupported 'educational' claims
Manipulative design aimed at the child
Hidden subscription terms (inferred)
Fear-based or guilt-based marketing (inferred; parents are already anxious: 71% of parents of children under 12 in Pew's survey were at least somewhat concerned about too much screen time)

evidence.note: Buyer role and anxiety are sourced (NN/g Life Online research with 100+ participants in 6 cities; Pew survey of 3,640 US parents, 2020). NN/g cautions its study does not show whether device overuse harms children. Density, motion, contrast and font size are inferred general-adult defaults, since I found no parent-specific tests.

modifies.buyer: A buying group, typically 6–10 stakeholders, not one person; per Gartner, buyers spend only about 17% of the purchase journey meeting suppliers and 67% prefer a rep-free experience
trustSignals: Consistency between website claims and what sales says
avoid: Hiding pricing entirely
Forcing a sales conversation for basic information
Vague, jargon-heavy copy and incomplete product descriptions
Pushy tactics such as constant promotions, which NN/g linked to distrust
Inconsistent information between website and sellers (69% of surveyed buyers reported this)

evidence.note: NN/g B2B study and Gartner surveys. Gartner figures other than the March 2026 survey (nearly 650 buyers) and the 69% discrepancy finding were reached through secondary summaries.

modifies.buyer: An individual developer or tech lead who evaluates first (usually via a free trial), then an engineering manager or procurement; peer recommendation weighs heavily (Stack Overflow's survey: about 72–75% evaluate by starting a free trial, about 68–73% ask peers, about 61–63% use communities)
trustSignals: Complete, findable documentation (lack of documentation was the top obstacle to consuming APIs in Postman's surveys, 52–55%)
Reliability and security information (Postman: more than 7 in 10 cited reliability, security, performance and documentation as top pre-integration factors)
avoid: Marketing fluff in place of technical detail
Sign-up walls in front of documentation
Contact-sales-only pricing for basic tiers
Black-box claims (developers report low trust in unverified outputs)
Autoplay media and pop-ups (inferred)

evidence.note: Stack Overflow Developer Survey figures are taken from Stack Overflow's own marketer-facing summaries, which cite two survey years with slightly different percentages. Postman figures come from press releases and third-party write-ups of its State of the API reports (2020, 2021, 2023). Density, motion, contrast and font size are inferred.

modifies.buyer: The individual visitor; default assumption when no specific audience is known
trustSignals: Clean, professional visual design (46.1% of credibility comments in Fogg et al.)
Clear about, contact and policy pages
Text contrast of at least 4.5:1 and targets of at least 24 x 24 CSS px (WCAG 2.2 AA)
avoid: Burying the value proposition below the fold: about 57% of viewing time is above the fold and 74% in the first two screenfuls
Text-heavy blocks
Small tap targets and low-contrast text
Autoplay media and intrusive pop-ups

evidence.note: Grounded in NN/g eyetracking, Fogg et al. and W3C standards. WCAG defines accessibility floors, not conversion outcomes.
